value: Which physiological mechanisms operate on which time scales, and how do those time scales map onto the behavioural categories of working, short-term and long-term memory and onto the different forms of learning?

Argues that multiple time scales are a necessary consequence of the nervous system's capacity and speed limits, and lays out an explicit map linking working, short-term and long-term memory to activity traces, short-term plasticity, long-term plasticity and structural plasticity, marking each proposed link as experimentally or only theoretically supported.

quote: In this prospect we review these mechanisms with respect to their time scale and propose relations between mechanisms in learning and memory and their underlying physiological basis.
The strategy of the nervous system to overcome these limitations apparently is to use different time scales in the memorization process.

value: Forgetting on finite, graded storage times acts as an implicit compression algorithm, holding down both the capacity needed and the time to retrieve an item
quote: Hence, the nervous system is implicitly performing an algorithm by means of its finite storage time (i.e., by forgetting meaningless items) to more efficiently store and access data.

value: New memories overwrite and interfere with old ones, which lowers the network's capacity demand but destroys important items - the cost that multiple time scales exist to avoid
quote: Another possibility is the permanent overwriting or interference with old memories, which in turn reduces the capacity requirements of the network [see, e.g., (Mézard et al. 1986; Sikström 2002) for Hopfield models] but also deletes important memories.

value: Hebbian potentiation feeds back on itself - a strengthened synapse drives the postsynaptic neuron harder, which strengthens it further - producing runaway weight growth unless a counteracting mechanism is present
quote: Independently of the interpretation of Hebbian plasticity this mechanism results in divergent dynamics: if an input drives the firing of a postsynaptic neuron, then plasticity potentiates the synaptic weight and, in this way, causes a stronger input drive, which in turn generates more potentiation, and so on.

value: An organism evolves a given memory time scale only if its lifespan and environment exert evolutionary pressure for correlations at that scale
quote: For example, an organism that lives only for a few weeks will never “feel” the evolutionary pressure to develop long-term memories for planning food harvesting for the winter season.

value: Spike-triggered calcium influx into the presynaptic terminal raises release probability (facilitation) while use depletes the vesicle pool (depression), giving synapses a seconds-long memory
quote: The arrival of spikes at the synapse leads to a calcium influx into the presynaptic terminal and, thus, to an increase in the release probability (synaptic facilitation).
Working memory, a term coined by Miller et al. (1960), is a theoretical concept believed to underlie human thought processes.
The memory type with the longest time scale is long-term memory, which operates on a scale of days to years—perhaps even for an entire lifetime.
Note that this capacity might be increased by a process called chunking, whereby atomic information is combined into larger compounds, with the chunks being stored somewhere else.
Detectability means that there are changes at the synaptic level after an animal has learned or memorized something (e.g., Rioult-Pedotti et al., 1998; Whitlock et al., 2006).
Retrograde alteration implies varying the synaptic strength in such a way that a learned memory item can be “reprogrammed” to become another memory (Pastalkova et al. 2006).

Beside synaptic plasticity, which adapts the synaptic strength between neurons, structural plasticity decides which synapse is created and which is deleted (Holtmaat and Svoboda 2009; Caroni et al. 2012).

These so-called eligibility traces (Hull 1943; Rall 1967) are used in many approaches [e.g., Sutton (1988); Sutton and Barto (1998); Suri and Schultz (1999); Porr and Wörgötter (2003)] to bridge time gaps in learning algorithms, but the physiological basis of longer traces is unclear.

Intrinsic plasticity (Triesch 2007; Mozzachiodi and Byrne 2009; Gründemann and Häusser 2010) describes a mechanism that changes, based on the neuron’s activity history, a neuron’s input–output activity relation, thereby leading to distinct neuronal responses for different “memorized” activities.

The fact that these synaptic changes due to LTP/LTD become permanent for several hours depends on a mechanism called synaptic tagging (Frey and Morris 1997; Clopath et al. 2008; Redondo and Morris 2011). Here, highly active synapses are tagged for long-lasting potentiation.

The abstract idea of this concept is that a complex network of calculating identities (e.g., neurons) is so diverse that each task is solved somewhere within the network (Maass et al. 2002; Buonomano and Maass 2009; Maass 2010).
Here, the synaptic efficiency of all inputs to a neuron increases/ decreases if the activity of this neuron is lower/higher than a target activity (Davis 2006).

value: The three memory concepts occupy non-overlapping time scales: working memory spans milliseconds to minutes, short-term memory minutes to days, and long-term memory days to years.
quote: Whereas the time scale of working memory is from milliseconds to minutes, short-term memory stores items on a time scale of minutes to days.

value: Having several distinct storage time scales, rather than one, protects important memories from being erased by the overwriting and interference that ongoing storage would otherwise cause.
quote: Thus, different time scales could avoid the deletion of important information.

value: Robot experiments in which a fast adaptation process is combined with a slow one produce more complex behaviour than either time scale alone.
quote: Furthermore, if different time scales interact, then one observes in robot experiments that more complex behaviors can be obtained.

value: Caenorhabditis elegans shows synaptic plasticity but no experience-based structural plasticity, so organisms do not necessarily exploit all available time scales.
quote: For example, no experiencebased structural plasticity [(Chen et al. 2006; Varshney et al. 2011), long time scale] was found in the “simple” worm Caenorhabditis elegans, while it can still make use of synaptic plasticity [(Dabbish and Raizen 2011), shorter time scale].

value: Of the proposed memory-physiology links, working memory-to-activity and long-term-memory-to-structural-plasticity have experimental support, whereas the classic long-term-memory-to-long-term-plasticity link is still disputed.
quote: In summary, it is interesting to note that there exist experimental support for links between (1) working memory and activity and (2) long-term memory and structural plasticity, but the very early proposed link between long-term memory and long-term plasticity (Hebb 1949) is still under debate

value: Of Martin et al.'s four criteria for tying plasticity to memory, mimicry has never been experimentally realised.
quote: So far, mimicry cannot be experimentally induced.

value: Rats in enriched environments grow significantly more dendritic spines than controls, which the authors read as experimental evidence linking long-term memory to structural plasticity.
quote: When rats experience enriched environments, their dendrites start to build significantly more spines than in a control environment (Xu et al. 2009; Yang et al. 2009).

value: Adding synaptic scaling with a quadratic weight dependence to a generic plasticity rule can be shown mathematically to stabilise weight development.
quote: It can be shown mathematically that adding synaptic scaling with quadratic weight dependence to generic plasticity rules stabilizes weight development (Tetzlaff et al. 2011).

value: Structural plasticity is modelled only computationally because no analytical models of network topology change exist yet.
